summary.text: Introduce the companion Lucas sequence \(v_0=2,\ v_1=-2,\ v_{n+2}=-2v_{n+1}-16v_n\), and prove from the recurrence that \(2a_n=2^n v_{n+1}+2^{3n+2}(1-(-1)^n)\). Representing \(v_n\) via \((-1+\sqrt{-15})^n\) gives the doubling identity \(v_n^2=v_{2n}+2\cdot16^n\), which simplifies the odd-index formula to \(a_{2n+1}=(2^n v_{n+1})^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n. \tag{1}
\]
We will prove the stronger explicit identity
\[
 a_{2n+1}=\bigl(2^n v_{n+1}\bigr)^2, \tag{2}
\]
where \((v_n)\) is the auxiliary integer sequence
\[
v_0=2,\qquad v_1=-2,\qquad
v_{n+2}=-2v_{n+1}-16v_n. \tag{3}
\]
Since the right side of (2) is the square of an integer, this will prove the conjecture.

We first establish a doubling identity for \(v_n\). To do so, work in the quadratic ring consisting of formal expressions \(r+s\delta\), with \(r,s\in\mathbb Z\), where \(\delta^2=-15\). Multiplication is therefore
\[
(r+s\delta)(u+w\delta)=(ru-15sw)+(rw+su)\delta.
\]
For each \(n\ge 0\), define integers \(x_n,y_n\) by
\[
(-1+\delta)^n=x_n+y_n\delta.
\]
Equivalently, these integers are given recursively by
\[
x_0=1,\quad y_0=0,
\]
\[
x_{n+1}=-x_n-15y_n,\qquad y_{n+1}=x_n-y_n. \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, (4) is exactly the result of multiplying \(x_n+y_n\delta\) by \(-1+\delta\).

The quadratic norm of \(x_n+y_n\delta\) gives
\[
x_n^2+15y_n^2=16^n. \tag{5}
\]
This can also be checked directly by induction. It is true for \(n=0\), and (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1}^2+15y_{n+1}^2
 &=(-x_n-15y_n)^2+15(x_n-y_n)^2\\
 &=16x_n^2+240y_n^2\\
 &=16(x_n^2+15y_n^2),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (5).

Multiplication of the powers \((-1+\delta)^m\) and \((-1+\delta)^n\) also gives the addition formulas
\[
x_{m+n}=x_mx_n-15y_my_n, \tag{6}
\]
\[
y_{m+n}=x_my_n+y_mx_n. \tag{7}
\]
These formulas follow immediately from the displayed multiplication rule; alternatively, they follow by induction on \(n\) from (4). Taking \(m=n\) in (6), we obtain
\[
x_{2n}=x_n^2-15y_n^2. \tag{8}
\]

We next identify the auxiliary sequence \(v_n\) with \(2x_n\). We have
\[
2x_0=2=v_0,
\]
and, since (4) gives \(x_1=-1\),
\[
2x_1=-2=v_1.
\]
Moreover, applying (4) twice yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+2}
 &=-x_{n+1}-15y_{n+1}\\
 &=-(-x_n-15y_n)-15(x_n-y_n)\\
 &=-14x_n+30y_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
-2x_{n+1}-16x_n
=-2(-x_n-15y_n)-16x_n
=-14x_n+30y_n.
\]
Thus
\[
x_{n+2}=-2x_{n+1}-16x_n.
\]
The sequence \(2x_n\) consequently has the same first two values and the same recurrence as \(v_n\), so induction gives
\[
v_n=2x_n \qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{9}
\]

Now combine (5), (8), and (9). We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_n^2
 &=4x_n^2,\\
v_{2n}+2\cdot16^n
 &=2x_{2n}+2(x_n^2+15y_n^2)\\
 &=2(x_n^2-15y_n^2)+2(x_n^2+15y_n^2)\\
 &=4x_n^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
v_n^2=v_{2n}+2\cdot16^n \qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{10}
\]
This is the doubling identity that will turn the odd terms of \(a_n\) into squares.

We now derive a useful closed expression for twice \(a_n\). Define
\[
P_n=2^n v_{n+1}+2^{3n+2}\bigl(1-(-1)^n\bigr). \tag{11}
\]
We claim that
\[
2a_n=P_n \qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{12}
\]
To prove this, we first show that \(P_n\) obeys the same fourth-order recurrence as \(a_n\).

Rewrite the second term in (11) as
\[
2^{3n+2}\bigl(1-(-1)^n\bigr)
=4\bigl(8^n-(-8)^n\bigr). \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(P_n=Q_n+G_n\), where
\[
Q_n=2^n v_{n+1},
\qquad
G_n=4\bigl(8^n-(-8)^n\bigr). \tag{14}
\]

From the recurrence (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{n+2}
 &=2^{n+2}v_{n+3}\\
 &=2^{n+2}(-2v_{n+2}-16v_{n+1})\\
 &=-4\bigl(2^{n+1}v_{n+2}\bigr)-64\bigl(2^nv_{n+1}\bigr)\\
 &=-4Q_{n+1}-64Q_n.
\end{aligned} \tag{15}
\]
Applying the relation \(Q_{k+2}+4Q_{k+1}+64Q_k=0\) at the appropriate shifted indices, or simply taking the difference of that relation at index \(n+2\) and \(64\) times the relation at index \(n\), gives
\[
Q_{n+4}+4Q_{n+3}-256Q_{n+1}-4096Q_n=0. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, the two \(Q_{n+2}\)-terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
0={}&(Q_{n+4}+4Q_{n+3}+64Q_{n+2})\\
&\quad-64(Q_{n+2}+4Q_{n+1}+64Q_n)\\
={}&Q_{n+4}+4Q_{n+3}-256Q_{n+1}-4096Q_n.
\end{aligned}
\]

The geometric sequences \(8^n\) and \((-8)^n\) satisfy the same fourth-order relation. For either \(r=8\) or \(r=-8\),
\[
r^4+4r^3-256r-4096=0. \tag{17}
\]
Equivalently, this follows from the factorization
\[
T^4+4T^3-256T-4096=(T^2-64)(T^2+4T+64), \tag{18}
\]
since \(r^2=64\). Multiplying (17) by \(r^n\) shows
\[
r^{n+4}+4r^{n+3}-256r^{n+1}-4096r^n=0.
\]
Taking four times the difference of this identity for \(r=8\) and \(r=-8\), we obtain
\[
G_{n+4}+4G_{n+3}-256G_{n+1}-4096G_n=0. \tag{19}
\]
Adding (16) and (19), and using \(P_n=Q_n+G_n\), proves
\[
P_{n+4}=-4P_{n+3}+256P_{n+1}+4096P_n. \tag{20}
\]

It remains to compare the first four values. From (3),
\[
v_2=-2v_1-16v_0=4-32=-28,
\]
\[
v_3=-2v_2-16v_1=56+32=88,
\]
and
\[
v_4=-2v_3-16v_2=-176+448=272.
\]
Using these values in (11), we get
\[
P_0=v_1+4(1-1)=-2=2a_0,
\]
\[
P_1=2v_2+2^5(1-(-1))=-56+64=8=2a_1,
\]
\[
P_2=4v_3+2^8(1-1)=352=2a_2,
\]
and
\[
P_3=8v_4+2^{11}(1-(-1))=2176+4096=6272=2a_3.
\]
The sequences \(P_n\) and \(2a_n\) therefore agree at indices \(0,1,2,3\), and both satisfy (20), because multiplying (1) by \(2\) gives that recurrence for \(2a_n\). Strong induction now proves (12): if equality is known at all indices below \(n+4\), then (1) and (20), using the already known equalities at \(n+3,n+1,n\), give equality at \(n+4\).

We finally specialize (12) to an odd index. Since \((-1)^{2n+1}=-1\), formula (11) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2a_{2n+1}
 &=P_{2n+1}\\
 &=2^{2n+1}v_{2n+2}
   +2^{3(2n+1)+2}\bigl(1-(-1)^{2n+1}\bigr)\\
 &=2^{2n+1}v_{2n+2}+2^{6n+6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both terms on the right are divisible by \(2\), so cancellation of the common factor \(2\) in the integers yields
\[
a_{2n+1}=2^{2n}v_{2n+2}+2^{6n+5}. \tag{21}
\]
Apply the doubling identity (10) with \(n+1\) in place of \(n\). It says
\[
v_{n+1}^2=v_{2n+2}+2\cdot16^{n+1},
\]
or equivalently
\[
v_{2n+2}=v_{n+1}^2-2\cdot16^{n+1}
=v_{n+1}^2-2\cdot2^{4n+4}. \tag{22}
\]
Substituting (22) into (21), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}
 &=2^{2n}\bigl(v_{n+1}^2-2\cdot2^{4n+4}\bigr)+2^{6n+5}\\
 &=2^{2n}v_{n+1}^2-2^{2n+1+4n+4}+2^{6n+5}\\
 &=2^{2n}v_{n+1}^2-2^{6n+5}+2^{6n+5}\\
 &=2^{2n}v_{n+1}^2\\
 &=\bigl(2^n v_{n+1}\bigr)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (2). Thus, for every nonnegative integer \(n\), the integer
\[
b_n=2^n v_{n+1}
\]
satisfies \(a_{2n+1}=b_n^2\). Hence every odd-indexed term \(a(2n+1)\) of A113254 is a perfect square.
